name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how a clinical or operational setting prepares for, deploys, and monitors artificial intelligence systems. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points, and the people and processes around each tool. The audit is not a one-time product check but a recurring assessment of readiness, from procurement through post-deployment surveillance. It sits within governance, compliance, and medical device security rather than model development itself.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how a clinical or operational setting prepares for, deploys, and monitors artificial intelligence systems. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points, and the people and processes around each tool. The audit is not a one-time product check but a recurring assessment of readiness, from procurement through post-deployment surveillance. It sits within governance, compliance, and medical device security rather than model development itself.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same infrastructure that supports clinical AI: electronic health record integrations, model registries, data pipelines, and monitoring dashboards. It also depends on documentation systems such as risk management files, standard operating procedures, and vendor contracts. In practice, the audit may use a lightweight registry or spreadsheet, but it must be able to trace each model to its version, training data, and deployment environment. The site's tracking of 1000 medical AI models and 732 AI tools reflects the scale of inventory that an audit may need to cover.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by walking through each stage of the AI lifecycle with a checklist tied to regulatory and safety expectations. Auditors interview clinical owners, technical staff, and compliance officers, then sample records to confirm that what is documented matches what is running. They test change management, access controls, and incident response, and they review performance reports for drift or unexpected behavior. The method is closer to a quality system audit than a code review, though it may include spot checks of model outputs and data quality.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this audit center on patient safety, data protection, and accountability when a model contributes to a decision. The audit examines whether patients are informed, whether data use is lawful and limited to the stated purpose, and whether there is a clear owner for each model in use. It also checks that adverse events and near misses are logged and escalated, and that liability and insurance arrangements are understood. The site's tracking of active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies is a reminder that governance records can become evidence, so the audit treats documentation as a control, not a formality.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI enablement audit is moving from a periodic project to a continuous function embedded in clinical governance. As more models are deployed and updated, audits will rely on automated evidence collection, such as model cards, audit logs, and real-time performance feeds. Regulators are likely to expect evidence of ongoing monitoring rather than point-in-time approval, and procurement teams will ask for auditability before purchase. The direction is toward a standing audit trail that can answer, at any moment, which models are live, what they are doing, and who is responsible.
